clinicalPearls: The acquired form arises in patients on long-term dialysis, in whom beta-2 microglobulin, normally cleared by the kidney, accumulates and is poorly removed by conventional membranes.
The phenotype is predominantly osteoarticular, comprising carpal tunnel syndrome, chronic large-joint arthropathy (especially the shoulders) and destructive spondyloarthropathy.
Subchondral bone cysts (amyloidomas) and an increased risk of pathological fracture are characteristic radiological findings.
Risk rises with duration of dialysis and older age at commencement, and disease was more common before high-flux and more biocompatible membranes.
Carpal tunnel syndrome is frequently the earliest manifestation and is often bilateral.
A distinct rare hereditary form results from a variant beta-2 microglobulin (Asp76Asn) that causes visceral, gastrointestinal and autonomic disease unrelated to dialysis.
Successful renal transplantation lowers beta-2 microglobulin levels and generally halts progression, and improved dialysis techniques reduce incidence.
reference.pathophysiology: Beta-2 microglobulin is the invariant light chain of MHC class I molecules and is normally filtered and catabolised by the kidney. In renal failure, and especially during prolonged dialysis with membranes that clear it inefficiently, serum concentrations rise many-fold. Over years the protein, sometimes modified by advanced glycation, aggregates into amyloid fibrils that deposit with particular affinity for synovium, tendon sheaths, articular cartilage and bone. The resulting infiltration produces carpal tunnel compression, erosive arthropathy and cystic bone lesions. In the rare hereditary variant, an unstable mutant protein deposits in the viscera independent of renal function.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of carpal tunnel syndrome
Other systemic amyloidoses such as AL and ATTR
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs or ultrasound showing subchondral cysts and synovial thickening
Nerve conduction studies for carpal tunnel syndrome
Synovial or bone biopsy with Congo red staining and amyloid typing where needed
Serum beta-2 microglobulin with review of dialysis modality and vintage
Serum free light chains and immunofixation to exclude AL amyloidosis
Genetic testing where a hereditary variant is suspected
redFlags: Destructive arthropathy or pathological fracture in a long-term dialysis patient
Visceral or autonomic symptoms suggesting the hereditary variant
reference.prognosis: In dialysis-related disease morbidity is largely musculoskeletal and progresses with dialysis vintage; renal transplantation arrests progression. The rare hereditary visceral form is slowly progressive and systemic.
pitfalls: Attributing shoulder or wrist symptoms in dialysis patients to age or overuse rather than amyloid
Overlooking subchondral bone cysts as a fracture risk
Assuming all amyloid in a dialysis patient is beta-2 microglobulin without excluding AL
Failing to recognise the distinct hereditary variant
